section_summary: This section consists chiefly of 1940 diplomatic, military-intelligence, and naval reports monitoring Japanese personnel, shipping, commerce, propaganda, and diplomatic strategy throughout Latin America. Most posts found little unusual activity, but several reports highlighted Japanese plans to counter U.S. influence, expand trade and intelligence networks, recruit aviators, cultivate military ties, and investigate petroleum resources near the Panama Canal. The section also documents German and Italian influence, alleged irregularities within the Japanese Legation in Panama, and strong public opposition to Japanese petroleum technicians in Esmeraldas, Ecuador. A 1942 covering letter forwarding a sealed Chinese communication appears at the beginning.

subfiles.title: Forwarding a sealed communication from the Chinese Minister in Mexico
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: Dr. T. V. Soong, Chinese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards a sealed reply received through the American Embassy in Mexico City from the Chinese Minister there.
subfiles.summary: Department forwards a sealed communication for T. V. Soong, received through the Mexico City Embassy from the Chinese Minister in reply to Soong's letter.

subfiles.title: Movement of Japanese citizens through Guatemala City during December 1939
subfiles.from: U.S. Naval Attaché, Guatemala
subfiles.about: Reports the air travel and official or commercial affiliations of several Japanese nationals moving through Central America.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché report on December 1939 movements through Guatemala City of six Japanese, including Itoh, an import-export agent, and Yamamoto of Japan's Commerce Ministry.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in the Monterrey Consular District
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Monterrey despatch concerning Japanese fishing interests and trade in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Note: Japanese activity in the Monterrey district is unexceptional, centered on fishing rights on Mexico's west coast and oil purchases and sales of Japanese goods.

subfiles.title: Movement of Japanese citizens in Central America during March 1940
subfiles.doc_type: naval attaché report with duplicate copy
subfiles.from: F. H. Lamson-Scribner, U.S. Naval Attaché
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese diplomatic, commercial, and private travelers recorded in Central America during March 1940.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché report tracing six Japanese through Central America and Mexico in March 1940, with diplomatic roles, a prospective Nicaraguan barter treaty, and duplicate pages 4 and 5.

subfiles.title: Circular inquiry concerning unusual Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: All chiefs of mission in the American republics
subfiles.about: Requests immediate reports on suspicious Japanese activity and possible German attempts to encourage anti-Japanese resentment.
subfiles.summary: Circular asks missions to report unusual Japanese activities or shipping changes and signs of Germans exploiting nationalist resentment against Japanese residents.

subfiles.title: Reply from Caracas on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Caracas; signed Scott
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese or German activity in Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: Caracas reports no unusual Japanese activity or German encouragement of anti-Japanese feeling; the Japanese colony is about twenty people.

subfiles.title: Reply from Ciudad Trujillo on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Ciudad Trujillo; signed Hinkle
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese activity in the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.summary: Ciudad Trujillo reports no suspicious Japanese activity, normal NYK calls and no German anti-Japanese activity, since almost no Japanese live there.

subfiles.title: Reply from San José on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, San José; signed Hornibrook
subfiles.about: Reports no specified suspicious activity but comments on a Japanese special ambassador and German propaganda in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: San Jose reports no such activity; a Japanese special ambassador's party receives a cool welcome, while German propaganda on other subjects remains a concern.

subfiles.title: Reply from San Salvador on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, San Salvador; signed Frazer
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity, shipping, commerce, or German agitation in El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: San Salvador reports nothing new on Japanese activity, only two unofficial Japanese residents and fewer than fifty adult German Nazis, with no German interest in Japanese affairs.

subfiles.title: Reply from Bogotá on Japanese shipping
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Bogotá; signed Keith
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious activity except the planned resumption of an Osaka Shosen Kaisha service to Cartagena.
subfiles.summary: Bogota finds none of the specified activities, though Cartagena says the Osaka Shosen Line will resume service from Brazil with the Brazil Maru on June 22.

subfiles.title: Reply from Asunción on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Asunción; signed Howard
subfiles.about: States that there were no unusual Japanese activities to report.
subfiles.summary: This brief reply answers the Department's circular inquiry. It reports simply that no unusual activities had been detected.

subfiles.title: Reply from Guatemala City on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Guatemala City; signed Des Portes
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese activity beyond a previously reported matter and requests a response to an earlier telegram.
subfiles.summary: Guatemala City reports no suspicious Japanese activity beyond its May 9 telegram, and German agitation against Japanese there is impracticable.

subfiles.title: Reply from Montevideo on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Montevideo; signed Wilson
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity in Uruguay.
subfiles.summary: The mission acknowledges receipt of the circular through Buenos Aires. It states that there were no unusual activities to report.

subfiles.title: Reply from Santiago on Japanese activity and military proposals
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Santiago; signed Bowers
subfiles.about: Reports little Japanese activity in Chile and the rejection of Japanese military-exchange proposals.
subfiles.summary: Santiago reports few Japanese residents and no unusual ship movements; Chile rejected a Japanese military training mission and an offer to host ten Chilean officers in Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic conferences in the Western Hemisphere
subfiles.from: J. M. Churchill, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.about: Reports planned Japanese diplomatic conferences intended to coordinate policy in the Americas and reduce dependence on the United States.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Japan's Foreign Office, apparently at its Washington ambassador's initiative, called Western Hemisphere conferences to coordinate missions and reduce dependence on the U.S., including May in Rio and a later Washington one.

subfiles.title: Reply from Mexico City on Japanese and German activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Mexico City; signed Boal
subfiles.about: Reports no German agitation or unusual Japanese trade and shipping in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Mexican consular posts found no evidence that Germans provoke conflict between Mexicans and Japanese and no unusual Japanese commercial or shipping developments.

subfiles.title: Reply from Port-au-Prince on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Port-au-Prince; signed Mayer
subfiles.about: Reports no Japanese shipping, commerce, or activities in Haiti.
subfiles.summary: Port-au-Prince reports nothing to report; Haiti has no Japanese shipping, commerce or other activity.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping agency reportedly reserved for German sympathizers
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Bogotá; signed Keith
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese Legation would award an Osaka Line agency only to Germans or known German sympathizers.
subfiles.summary: Cartagena consul reports the Japanese Legation wrote that an Osaka Line agency would go only to Germans or German sympathizers.

subfiles.title: Japanese commerce and shipping in Nicaragua
subfiles.from: Meredith Nicholson, U.S. Legation, Managua
subfiles.about: Reports minimal Japanese activity in Nicaragua and intelligence that two Japanese Army aviation officers were recruiting pilots in the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Nicholson reports one Japanese merchant and occasional Japanese ships in Nicaragua; the Chinese consul-general says two Japanese Army aviation officers left Tokyo March 22 to recruit pilots in the Americas.

subfiles.title: Unusual and suspicious Japanese activities in Panama
subfiles.from: William Dawson, U.S. Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports a shipping-agency transfer, concern about German activity in the Canal Zone, and alleged financial irregularities at the Japanese Legation.
subfiles.summary: Dawson reports the NYK agency in Panama moved from Hapag Lloyd to an American firm, leaving the German agency intact, and relays rumors of a $20,000 Japanese Legation shortage and recalls.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Masao Matsumoto and Japanese Legation officials
subfiles.from: L. A. McIntire, Civil Intelligence Section, Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Describes alleged Japanese Legation embezzlement, recalls of officials, and an altercation aboard the Argentina Maru.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum alleges Matsumoto investigated a $20,000 Legation shortage causing recalls of Otani, Suzuki and Minister Midzusawa, who allegedly had drunken ex-fishermen provoke him aboard the Argentina Maru.

subfiles.title: Liquidation of German firms in Latin America
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, U.S. Embassy, Mexico
subfiles.about: Refers the Department to a commercial attaché's report indicating cordial German-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: Boal refers the Department to the commercial attaché's May 25 report on liquidating German firms in Latin America, suggesting German-Japanese relations stayed cordial.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Brazil
subfiles.from: Ware Adams for the U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese diplomatic conferences, shipping, trade, cotton purchases, and propaganda in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Embassy reports a conference of Japanese diplomats from Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru; moderate rise in shipping for cotton, steady trade, expanded propaganda, and a possible clearing agreement.

subfiles.title: German and Japanese activities in Pará
subfiles.from: Randolph Harrison, Jr., for the U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Transmits a vice-consular report on German and Japanese activities in Pará.
subfiles.summary: Embassy forwards the Para vice consul's May 21 report on Japanese commerce and German and Nazi organizing.

subfiles.title: Report from Pará on German and Japanese activities
subfiles.from: T. Muldrup Forsyth, American Vice Consul, Pará
subfiles.to: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports little Japanese activity but increased public visibility and organizing by Germans and Nazis in Pará.
subfiles.summary: Forsyth finds no unusual Japanese activity at Para; Germans are more conspicuous after European successes, and Nazis meet, but no German effort against the mostly rural Japanese was detected.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Transmits consular reports from Concepción and Valparaíso on Japanese activity in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Bowers submits Concepcion and Valparaiso consular replies assessing Japanese residents, firms, trade, shipping and prospects for anti-Japanese agitation.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Concepción
subfiles.from: Camden L. McLain, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports a small Japanese community and no suspicious activity in the Concepción district.
subfiles.summary: McLain identifies five known Japanese residents at Concepcion with no suspicious conduct, notes Japanese firms and a dairy, no Japanese shipping, and no anti-Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities and shipping at Valparaíso
subfiles.from: Renwick S. McNiece, American Consul
subfiles.about: Reports normal Japanese activity at Valparaíso and evaluates shipping, cargo, and the likelihood of racial agitation.
subfiles.summary: McNiece finds no suspicious Japanese activity at Valparaiso, notes reduced K.K.K. service and monthly NYK sailings, and considers German-inspired racial agitation unlikely.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in the Mexicali Consular District
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office, citing Moore at Mexicali
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report describing the small, established Japanese farming population around Mexicali.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Mexicali's Japanese residents are mostly small farmers and long-term legal residents, unlikely to cause U.S.-Mexican friction, though special agents might.

subfiles.title: German and Japanese activities in Bolivia
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, U.S. Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports little unusual Japanese activity but extensive concern about German military propaganda and foreign advisers in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Jenkins reports no exceptional Japanese conduct in Bolivia but describes Major Lehmann's propaganda among Army officers; Japanese matters include a sample arms shipment and a Mitsui view of the Lima disturbances.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum for Japanese-activities report
subfiles.from: Liaison Officer, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests that an attached report be forwarded to the Office of Naval Intelligence after War Department review.
subfiles.summary: State liaison officer sends an attachment to the War Department for onward transmission to Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in São Paulo and Santos
subfiles.from: Carol H. Foster, American Consul General, São Paulo
subfiles.to: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports unusually active Japanese propaganda and travel but generally normal trade and shipping in São Paulo and Santos.
subfiles.summary: Foster reports intensified Japanese propaganda and many travelers in Sao Paulo and Santos, modestly higher imports, stable shipping, only two cotton vessels expected, and no German anti-Japanese effort.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing cover sheet
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.to: Department officials including Duggan and Welles
subfiles.about: Routes a strictly confidential report concerning Japanese plans in the American republics.
subfiles.summary: State Department routing cover sheet for American Republics and Far Eastern Affairs divisions, marked strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Japanese plans for penetration in the American republics
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.to: Chief of Staff and listed recipients
subfiles.about: Summarizes intelligence on Japanese plans formulated at the May 1940 Rio de Janeiro diplomatic conference.
subfiles.summary: Miles reports Japanese diplomats in Rio reviewed activity in South America and planned measures to restrain American influence, with an attached memorandum of objectives sent to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Program adopted at the Japanese diplomatic conference in Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.from: Japanese Ambassador in Rio de Janeiro, as reported by U.S. intelligence
subfiles.about: Sets out a broad Japanese political, economic, intelligence, cultural, and organizational program for Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The program calls for cultivating influential politicians, countering American propaganda, cooperating selectively with Italy, Spain, and Portugal, strengthening military contacts, selling arms, and inviting missions from Chile. Economic measures include credit institutions, expanded commercial staffs, regulated exporters, infrastructure projects, resource surveys, manufacturing plants, and Japanese control of shipping agencies. It also proposes a Domei news office, stronger broadcasts, intelligence exchanges about communism, cultural agreements and exchanges, new diplomatic posts, and recurring inter-American conferences.

subfiles.title: No suspicious Japanese activities in Honduras
subfiles.from: John D. Erwin, U.S. Legation, Tegucigalpa
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity or German agitation in Honduras while noting gradually increasing Japanese trade.
subfiles.summary: Erwin reports almost no Japanese residents, no suspicious conduct, and no exceptional activity at Puerto Cortés or La Ceiba. Japanese textiles and other imports had increased gradually, but without a sudden change. Germans were keeping a low profile, and President Carías's pro-Allied government was expected to suppress hostile propaganda quickly.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese shipping changes, cultural diplomacy, and the absence of notable anti-Japanese sentiment in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Armour finds little resentment against Japanese in Argentina; Osaka Shosen altered its fleet, and Japan offered lavish facilities for five Argentine professors visiting Japan and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Japanese vessels touching at Argentine ports
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Lists Osaka Shosen Kaisha and Yamashita Line vessels serving Argentine ports.
subfiles.summary: List of Japanese vessels in the Argentine trade, including new Argentina Maru and Brazil Maru and several withdrawn ships.

subfiles.title: Compañía Minera Petrolera del Pacífico
subfiles.from: Boaz Long, U.S. Legation, Quito
subfiles.about: Transmits reports and commentary on Japanese geologists and an Ecuadorian petroleum-concession company operating in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Long forwards a warning and reports on Japanese technicians in Esmeraldas working for the Colombian-controlled Pacific Petroleum Mining Company, which may seek to trade concessions; he requests instructions.

subfiles.title: Anonymous warning about Japanese soldiers in Ecuador
subfiles.from: “Ecuatorianos, amantes de la Paz y tranquilidad”
subfiles.about: Alleges that Japanese soldiers disguised as agricultural workers were entering Ecuador to threaten the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: Anonymous Spanish letter alleges Japanese aviators posing as farmers in Esmeraldas, plans to bring thousands of soldiers near the Panama Canal, and an Italian-prepared fascist coup; it urges American intervention.

subfiles.title: Confidential comments on Japanese technicians and the Ecuadorian government
subfiles.from: Confidential adviser or informant
subfiles.about: Evaluates the anonymous warning and urges investigation and expulsion of Japanese petroleum technicians in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Informant says Spillmann and several Japanese are technicians for the Colombian-controlled oil company with large concessions, and recommends interrogation, expulsion and limits on Japanese role in Ecuadorian petroleum.

subfiles.title: El Día report on Japanese geologists in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Día
subfiles.about: Reports official confirmation that Japanese technicians were employed for mineral exploration because American experts were too expensive.
subfiles.summary: El Dia reports Japanese geologists working in Esmeraldas; Foreign Ministry sources say American technicians were too costly and deny political significance.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo article on the Esmeraldas oil concession
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese technicians working on an Esmeraldas oil concession might represent a broader penetration effort near the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: El Telegrafo says Ecuadorians hired Spillmann and seven Japanese for a large Esmeraldas oil concession; it questions the concessionaires, warns of strategic observation near the Canal, and urges investigation.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: Alfred T. Nester, American Consul, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Transmits Ecuadorian press reports on public reaction to Japanese activity in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Nester encloses translations of El Telegrafo and El Universo reports on opposition to Japanese technicians in Esmeraldas.

subfiles.title: El Universo report on the Esmeraldas protest
subfiles.from: El Universo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Reports police dispersal of a protest against a Japanese petroleum mission in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: El Universo: Esmeraldas residents protested a Japanese petroleum mission as dangerous immigration; police dispersed the crowd, and the party left under protection.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo report on suspected Japanese penetration
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Reports public alarm in Esmeraldas over alleged secret Japanese activity and plans for a protest meeting.
subfiles.summary: El Telegrafo: residents suspected secret Japanese maneuvers; police asked protesters to wait for government instructions, and El Cosmopolita accused unnamed interests of taking Japanese money.

subfiles.title: El Universo clipping on alleged dangerous Japanese activity in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Universo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Publishes allegations that Franz Spillmann and Japanese associates were seeking petroleum or gold under suspicious circumstances in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: El Universo clipping: claims that Spillmann misrepresented work at Tolita and returned with Japanese companions, a matter of national interest.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo clipping on public opposition in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Prints the Spanish original of the report on protests against alleged Japanese penetration.
subfiles.summary: El Telegrafo clipping on alarm over Japanese activity in Esmeraldas, with police seeking postponement of a demonstration and a planned Municipal Theatre meeting.

subfiles.title: Secret report on Japanese recruitment of aviators
subfiles.from: Gordon B. McCoy, Lieutenant Colonel, U.S. Army
subfiles.about: Relays intelligence that Japanese officers were ordered to recruit aviators or military personnel in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Secret report that two Japanese colonels were ordered to recruit aviators in Latin America; the analyst sees preparation for another theater, perhaps the Dutch East Indies, and recommends inquiry.

subfiles.title: Movements of Japanese nationals recorded by the Naval Attaché
subfiles.from: F. H. Lamson-Scribner, U.S. Naval Attaché, Guatemala
subfiles.about: Reports the movements and commercial roles of Shunichi Yamamoto, Yoshitaro Amano, and Y. Megurikami.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché report on Japanese travelers: Yamamoto promoting Mitsui compensation trade, Amano a fishing boat owner at Puntarenas, and Megurikami expected to transfer to Ecuador.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic approach to Latin American governments
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese instructions urging Latin American governments to resist dependence on the United States and remain politically impartial.
subfiles.summary: Chinese Minister relays four Japanese arguments to Latin American governments: diversify trade, develop Far Eastern commerce, avoid war-related agreements, and treat regions impartially; General Hay confirms a similar friendly approach.

subfiles.title: Transmitting a letter from the Chinese Minister in Havana
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Forwards Chinese intelligence about Japanese efforts to obstruct U.S. influence and the Havana Conference.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith transmits a July 16 letter from the Chinese Minister and notes that the Japanese chargé had recently sent identical coded messages to Japanese missions throughout the American republics. He suggests that the Chinese information might help the Office of Naval Intelligence decode those messages.

subfiles.title: Chinese warning about Japanese instructions for the Havana Conference
subfiles.from: Ti-Tsun Li, Chinese Minister in Cuba
subfiles.about: Warns that Japan instructed its Latin American diplomats to frustrate U.S. influence and undermine the Havana Conference.
subfiles.summary: Li reports Foreign Minister Arita ordered Japanese representatives to resist U.S. influence at the Havana Conference, and asks that the U.S. delegation be told and for an interview with Hull.

subfiles.title: Japanese firms in Mexico
subfiles.from: Mexico City report by McGregor
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Japanese firms and activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a June 28 Mexico City report on Japanese firms.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Veracruz
subfiles.from: Veracruz despatch by Cochran
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on the end of a Japanese-backed petroleum venture and Japanese interest in strategic minerals.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: almost no Japanese activity in Veracruz, a Japanese-organized oil company ended, and an unconfirmed report of a Japanese traveler investigating mica and antimony in Oaxaca.
